question: I’m using a decision tree to predict loan approval, and the positive class is much less common for one protected group. How should I build and evaluate the model so I don’t confuse a good-looking classifier with a fair one?
answer:
Great question — the course material covers exactly this split between "performing well" and "being fair." Here's how to approach it using only what we've covered.

## 1. Don't let accuracy fool you

The performance-metrics slides open with the warning that "Accuracy may not be enough" and that errors on training data are an *optimistic* indication of future errors (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-eval-metrics/2025-06-09-perfmet-slides.pdf`, p.7). With a rare positive class this is acute: a confusion matrix built on your data can look fine because true negatives dominate. The slides list better options (p.20):

- **Precision** = TP/(TP+FP), **Recall/Sensitivity** = TP/(TP+FN)
- **Balanced Accuracy** = (sensitivity+specificity)/2
- **F1 Score** — the harmonic mean of precision and recall; the slides explicitly say F1 "is used when False Negatives and False Positives are more of a concern" and is "really best used on unbalanced datasets."
- **Prevalence** — the percentage of the positive class in the test set, and **Detection Rate**
- **AUC**, with the interpretation bands 0.9–1.0 excellent, 0.8–0.9 good, 0.7–0.8 fair, 0.6–0.7 poor, 0.5–0.6 fail (p.18)

The labs also build this habit in: step 5 of the classification lab is to "determine the baserate or prevalence for the classifier, what does this number mean?" (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2026-03-10-dt-class-lab.ipynb`) — do that *per group*, not just overall, so you know the base rates you're comparing against.

## 2. Remember the threshold is a choice

The classification cutoff (default 50%) "can be modified as an input if needed" (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-eval-metrics/2025-06-09-perfmet-slides.pdf`, p.10). The slides walk through thresholds of 0 and 100 to show how the whole confusion matrix shifts (pp.12–13), and the ROC curve is "essentially a graphical representation of the adjusted threshold values of the confusion matrix" (p.16). Since your minority group has few positives, the default threshold will almost certainly produce very different TPR/FPR for that group.

## 3. Evaluate fairness as a separate, group-wise step

The ethics slides frame this as **post-processing fairness**: checking whether "the errors of a model are similar across these groups," i.e. whether the model takes existing statistical variation into account "but not unfairly penalize the protected class variables in comparison to those that have similar profiles that don't represent a protected class — individual fairness" (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-value-ethics-slides.pptx`, slides 42–43).

Three methods are given (slides 54–56; also `raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-ml-bias-and-fairness-slides.pdf`, pp.25–27):

- **Demographic (proportional) parity** — do subgroups have the same proportion in the positive category? The slides use *your exact scenario*: a loan-worthiness model where equal approval percentages across race would satisfy this. But they warn it "is not overly useful… over simplified," because "false positive and true positive rates could vary between classes without our knowledge." So don't stop here.
- **Equality of odds** — are TPR *and* FPR the same across protected classes across different thresholds? "This is basically ROCs for each of the sub-groups." This is the one that directly answers your worry, because it's about how the errors are distributed.
- **Equal opportunity** — the extension that focuses only on the positive class; "we want the true positive rate to be the same for each protected class."

Practically: build a separate confusion matrix and ROC/AUC for each protected group, not one pooled one. The slides reference an IBM AIF360 credit-scoring tutorial as a worked example (slide 45).

## 4. Fixing it: threshold shift vs. pre-processing

The slides note "the idea behind these methods is to find the ideal threshold that allows the equations to be satisfied," but also that "threshold shift to satisfy any of these conditions can be difficult and sometimes not feasible given the data at hand." The alternative is to "control for these differences prior to developing our algorithms… methods weighting the variables ahead of time to avoid any potential bias" (`.../2024-10-29-ml-bias-and-fairness-slides.pdf`, pp.28–29).

## 5. Decision-tree-specific knob for the imbalance

The tree slides give a directly relevant hyperparameter: **minimum samples for a terminal node (leaf)** — "For imbalanced class problems, a lower value should be used since regions dominant with samples belonging to minority class will be much smaller in number" (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2022-10-20-decision-trees-slides-current.pptx`, slide 38). Trees are "often prone to overfitting," so tune depth, min samples per split, and max leaf nodes via cross-validation (slides 37–38), and consider Random Forest as an ensemble alternative.

## 6. Framing caution

The ethics slides close with: emphasize the *Science* part — define the question carefully, know your data sources are robust enough to generalize (if not, limit scope), know the limitations of the method, and remember that "machine learning systems designed to make decisions that are fully automated are very risky. The combination of human intuition and expertise alongside machine learning systems is a better approach" (p.30). For loan approval that's a substantive recommendation, not boilerplate.

---

**One gap to flag:** the slides define Equal Opportunity in prose as equalizing the *true positive rate*, but the same slide also prints "Precision – TP/TP+FP" next to it (slide 56 / p.27). I'm reporting that as-is; the material doesn't reconcile it. Also, the retrieved excerpts don't contain code for computing these fairness metrics group-by-group in Python — only the AIF360 link — so you'd need to ask about implementation separately.

question: I’m using k-means to group NBA players by performance so I can spot players who may be underpaid. Why would accuracy, F1, log loss, or ROC/AUC not be the right first way to judge the clustering, and what should I use instead? If I later turn the problem into a labeled classification task, how would the evaluation change?
answer:
## Short answer: those metrics need labels your clustering doesn't have

k-means is **unsupervised** machine learning: "The data inputs have (x) no target outputs (y)… We want to impose structure on the inputs (x) to say something meaningful about the data" (`raw/course/DS-3021/kmeans-clustering/2026-03-10-clustering-slides.pptx`). Clustering is described there as a technique for *finding similarity between groups*, where "Similarity needs to be defined… Usually a distance metric."

Accuracy, F1, log loss, and ROC/AUC, by contrast, are all built on knowing the true class of each observation. The course's performance-metrics deck frames them explicitly in those terms:

- The confusion matrix works because "we know because of the labels, what is fraud and not, so we can measure how good the model is classifying" (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-eval-metrics/2025-06-09-perfmet-slides.pdf`).
- TPR, FPR, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 are all computed from TP/FP/FN/TN counts (same file).
- ROC/AUC is "a graphical representation of the adjusted threshold values of the confusion matrix," i.e., it requires predicted *class probabilities* plus a true label to sweep a threshold against (same file).
- Log loss "measures the UNCERTAINTY of the probabilities of your model by comparing them to the true labels – CLASSIFICATION" (same file).

Your k-means output is a cluster assignment ("cluster: a vector indicating the cluster to which each point is allocated", clustering slides), not a probability of a known class. There's no "correct" cluster number 1 vs. 2 to compare against, so none of these metrics are even defined for the first pass.

## What to use instead

The course gives you a specific toolkit for cluster quality:

**1. Goals that define "good" clustering** — "Maximize the separation between clusters i.e. Maximize inter-cluster distance" and "Keep similar points in a cluster close together i.e. Minimize intra-cluster distance" (clustering slides, slide 31).

**2. Variance explained by clusters** — the ratio of inter-cluster variance to total variance:
`var_exp = betweenss / totss`, where `totss = withinss + betweenss` (clustering slides, slides 32–35). The kmeans outputs you'd use: `totss`, `withinss`, `tot.withinss`, `betweenss`, `size`, `centers`.

**3. Choosing k** — two methods are named: the **elbow method** ("Computes the percentage of variance explained by clusters for a range of cluster numbers… Looking for the kink in graph of inter-cluster variance / total variance"), and **NbClust**, which "Runs 30 different tests and provides 'majority vote' for the best number of clusters." The slides warn the elbow method is "Not guaranteed to work! It depends on the data in question" (slides 36–39).

**4. Silhouette scores** — the clustering lab explicitly asks you to "Evaluate the quality of the clustering using total variance explained and silhouette scores" and to "Determine the ideal number of clusters using the elbow method and the silhouette coefficient" (`raw/course/DS-3021/kmeans-clustering/2026-03-10-clustering-lab.ipynb`). *Note: the excerpts I have name silhouette scores but don't define or give a formula for them, so I can't give you the math from course material.*

**5. Don't forget scaling** — the lab is explicit: "You'll need to scale the variables before performing the clustering" (clustering lab). This matters because distance is the similarity metric.

**6. An independent business-value metric** — the readings stress "having a metric that is independent of the model that can be used to determine if the model is providing value," with the example "Market Clustering: Did sales increase" (`raw/course/DS-3021/knn/2024-10-29-machine-learning-III-reading.pdf`). For your scout, the real test is whether the under/overpaid labels you derive lead to useful signings — the clustering lab asks you to justify your own cutoffs for the good/maybe/bad player categories.

## If you convert it to a labeled classification task

Once you have a target variable — "the variable we are trying to predict" (same reading) — the whole evaluation picture changes, and *then* the metrics you listed become the right ones:

- **Establish prevalence first.** "The proportion of a particular population found to be in the positive class." The metrics lab makes this a required step: "make sure to calculate the prevalence to provide a reference for some of these measures" (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-eval-metrics/2025-06-09-model-metrics-lab.md`). The perfmet slides show why: a model that always predicts the majority class can hit "28/30 = 93% accuracy. This is misleading."
- **Build a confusion matrix**, then derive Accuracy, TPR/Sensitivity, FPR/(1−Specificity), Precision, Recall, Balanced Accuracy, F1, Log Loss, Kappa, and ROC/AUC (perfmet slides). AUC bands given: 0.9–1.0 Excellent, 0.8–0.9 Good, 0.7–0.8 Fair, 0.6–0.7 Poor, 0.5–0.6 Fail.
- **Pick metrics that match your question.** F1 "is used when False Negatives and False Positives are more of a concern. Also really best used on unbalanced datasets." For your use case, a false positive (signing someone the model called underpaid who isn't) costs differently than a false negative (missing a bargain) — the metrics lab asks exactly this: "are there a few that seem more important given the question you are asking? Why?"
- **Threshold is a choice, not a given.** "The cutoff point that is predetermined… is 50% but can be modified as an input if needed" (perfmet slides). This mirrors the clustering lab's instruction that you decide and justify your category cutoffs.
- **Evaluate on held-out data.** "Accuracy is better measured using test data that was not used to build the classifier"; training error is "optimistic" and is called resubstitution error (perfmet slides).

One honest caveat: the excerpts don't walk through the specific step of turning k-means cluster assignments into classification labels for the NBA problem. The lab frames it as using clustering plus visualizations of variables "most correlated with Salary" to reason about over/underpayment, and the write-up is where you justify your cutoffs — not as a supervised model with ROC curves.

It gives the exact clustering alternatives taught in the course: minimizing within‑cluster distance / maximizing between‑cluster distance, variance‑explained (betweenss/totss), the elbow method and NbClust, silhouette score, and the importance of scaling — all of which are explicitly recommended in the clustering slides and lab. For the supervised conversion it correctly summarizes the course guidance (compute prevalence, confusion matrix, derive accuracy/precision/recall/F1/log‑loss/AUC, choose metrics that match the business question, adjust thresholds, and evaluate on held‑out data). The response also responsibly notes a limitation in the ingested materials (they do not present the detailed mechanics of turning cluster labels into supervised labels), which is explicitly flagged in the answer. question: When tuning a random forest for a binary classification problem, how do choices like the number of trees and number of features considered at each split relate to the evaluation metrics I should report for the final model?
answer:
## Short answer

In this course the two things are linked through **out-of-bag (OOB) error as the tuning criterion** and a **separate, pre-chosen evaluation metric set for the final model**. The hyperparameters control the bias/variance behavior of the forest; the metrics you report should reflect the *cost structure* of your particular binary problem, and should be chosen *before* training.

## What the tuning knobs actually do

From the ensemble slides (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2020-11-09-ensemble-rf-slides.pptx`), Random Forest is a combination of bagging and boosting-like behavior, and the main tuning parameters are:

- **Number of variables used for each tree / at each split** ("kinda boosting" — *reduces bias*)
- **Number of trees in the forest** (bagging — *reduces variance*, less overfitting)
- **Size of the samples used in the bagging process**

The same slide deck notes that bagging works by "bootstrap aggregation" to reduce the complexity of models that tend to overfit, and that drawing random subsets of features is what keeps the trees uncorrelated — "that's the goal."

The decision-tree slides (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2022-10-20-decision-trees-slides-current.pptx`) add a useful caution about `max_features`: "A typical value is the square root of total number of available features. A higher number typically leads to over-fitting but is dependent on the problem as well." Max depth, min samples per leaf, and max leaf nodes "should be tuned using cross validation."

## How tuning was done in the class example

In the RF lecture notebook (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2026-08-31-rf-lecture-notebook.ipynb`), tuning is done by sweeping a parameter and plotting **OOB error**:

```python
max_features_list = [1,2,...,10]
forest_list2 = [RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_features=n, bootstrap=True,
                max_samples=100, min_samples_leaf=5, oob_score=True, ...).fit(X_train, y_train)
                for n in max_features_list]
oob_errors1 = [1 - i.oob_score_ for i in forest_list2]
plt.plot(max_features_list, oob_errors1)
```

with the comment: "Looking at the OOB error graph, 4 seems to be the right value to use in our random forest **without overfitting**." So OOB error is the *selection* metric; it is cheap because it comes free from the bagging process, and the same notebook uses `1 - oob_score_` as "model error."

The RF lab (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2026-08-31-rf-lab.ipynb`) follows exactly this sequence: build a default model → report "precision, recall, and accuracy… out of bag error rate… confusion matrix" → "Select the optimal number of trees" → "Select the optimal number of features" → "Compare the new tree to the original tree. What is the difference in the OOBE and confusion matrix?" → "Predict with the test set and discuss the model's performance, include the ROC curve and AUC."

That's the structure to copy: **tune on OOB (training-side), report on a held-out test set.**

## Which metrics to report, and why they interact with tuning

1. **Pick the metric first.** The lifecycle reading (`raw/course/MLBook/ml-foundations/2026-05-21-ds-lifecycle.ipynb`) is explicit: "It is critical that you work to establish why and which evaluation measure you plan to use ahead of the training process. This allows you and your team to discuss benchmarks for performance which in real world scenarios translate in the amount of risk (error) you are willing to accept." The same source lists accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and AUC as the common choices, and notes evaluation is what detects overfitting vs. underfitting.

2. **Match the metric to the error cost.** The RF lecture notebook motivates ROC/AUC this way: "It's OK if we classify someone who is pregnant as not pregnant, but we can have a big lawsuit on our hands if we falsely predict that someone is pregnant when in reality they are not. Let's see how our relative true positives compare to the false positives. To do that we'll need to plot a ROC curve." It then uses `RocCurveDisplay.from_estimator(...)` and picks a threshold via `np.argmax(tpr - fpr)`.

3. **Class imbalance changes the metric.** Both the DT slide decks warn that real-world datasets are often heavily imbalanced (fraud ~2%, intrusion detection ~.0001%) and that "standard algorithms function inefficiently" there (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2022-10-20-decision-trees-slides-current.pptx`). Plain accuracy would be misleading in those cases; the DT classification notebook correspondingly refits on `roc_auc` and also tracks `recall` and `balanced_accuracy` (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2025-02-13-decision-trees-lecture-notebook.ipynb`), and if you use `GridSearchCV` you can pass a scoring list and `refit=` the metric you actually care about.

4. **Threshold choice is separate from hyperparameter choice.** Note the ordering in the lecture notebook: the forest is tuned first (OOB), then the probability threshold is optimized against the ROC. The DT notebook has the same idea with its `adjust_thres` function. So "number of trees" and "max_features" don't by themselves fix precision/recall — the operating threshold does.

## Practical recipe for your model

- Tune `n_estimators` and `max_features` by plotting OOB error; stop adding trees once the OOB curve flattens, and avoid pushing `max_features` high since that trends toward overfitting.
- Report, on the **test** set: confusion matrix, precision, recall, accuracy (or balanced accuracy if imbalanced), plus ROC curve and AUC. Report OOB error for the training process.
- Also report feature importances, and cross-check with **permutation importance** — the lab explicitly asks you to compare the two and explain discrepancies; the slides note importance comes from OOB error and average decrease in Gini impurity, with permutation (shuffling a variable and watching model error) as the alternative (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2020-11-09-ensemble-rf-slides.pptx`, `raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2026-08-31-rf-lab.ipynb`).

## One caveat

The retrieved material does **not** give an explicit rule for how the *choice* of evaluation metric should change *which* hyperparameter values you select (e.g., whether optimizing for recall should push `max_features` in a particular direction). What it does say is that OOB error is the tuning criterion in the RF examples, and that the reporting metric must be justified in advance based on the risk you're willing to accept. If you want to tune directly against recall or AUC rather than OOB error, that's the `GridSearchCV(..., scoring=[...], refit='roc_auc')` pattern from the decision-tree notebooks, applied to an RF estimator — but the course notebooks demonstrate that pattern for single trees, not for the random forest.

question: If I’m using player performance and salary data to find underpaid players with k-means, but I also want a regression tree to predict salary or revenue, how should my preprocessing and model evaluation change between the two methods?
answer:
## Short answer
The two methods differ most in (1) whether you must scale, and (2) what "evaluation" even means — cluster-quality metrics vs. prediction-error metrics on held-out data.

---

### 1. Preprocessing

**k-means (NBA performance + salary):**
- **Scaling is required.** The clustering lab explicitly instructs: *"You'll need to scale the variables before performing the clustering"* (`raw/course/DS-3021/kmeans-clustering/2026-03-10-clustering-lab.ipynb`). The general bootcamp reading reinforces that many DS approaches require normalization "so comparison between variables is possible," and that the course mostly uses a min–max scaler that maintains variance but rescales values between 0 and 1 (`raw/course/DS-3021/data-prep/2024-10-29-ml-bootcamp-II-reading.pdf`).
- **Drop duplicate/unneeded variables** before clustering, and watch out for **non-traditional characters in player names**, which break certain graphs (clustering lab).
- You also have to **justify which variables you include** in the model (clustering lab).

**Regression tree (salary / gross revenue):**
- **No scaling needed.** The regression lab is blunt about it: *"you don't need to scale the data, because DTs don't require this to be done, they make local greedy decisions"* (`raw/course/DS-3021/dt-regression/2026-03-10-dt-regression-lab-v2.ipynb`). The decision-tree slides say the same at a conceptual level: trees "require little data preparation. Other techniques often require data normalization, dummy variables need to be created..." (`raw/course/DS-3021/dt-regression/2022-03-24-decision-trees-regression-slides.pptx`).
- Instead, your prep steps are: make sure variables are **classified correctly and collapse factor levels** as needed, **handle missing values**, and **examine the range/variance/distribution of the target** — if it isn't normally distributed you may want to transform it (both `2026-03-10-dt-regression-lab-v2.ipynb` and `2025-09-25-dt-regression-lab.ipynb`).
- You need an explicit **train/tune/test split (80/10/10)** and a **k-fold object for cross-validation** (same labs). Note the clustering lab asks for no such partition.

---

### 2. Evaluation

**k-means:** evaluate the *clustering structure*, not prediction error. The lab asks you to:
- compute **total variance explained** and **silhouette scores**,
- determine the ideal **k** using the **elbow method** and the **silhouette coefficient**, visualize the elbow, retrain with the recommended k, and re-evaluate variance explained and silhouette (`...kmeans-clustering/2026-03-10-clustering-lab.ipynb`).
- Interpretation is then done by eye/graph — the lab suggests plotting variables most correlated with salary and defining your own over/underpaid cutoffs, which you must justify.

**Regression tree:** evaluate *predictive error on held-out data*. The lab sequence is:
- choose **several scoring metrics** and a hyperparameter to optimize (e.g., `max_depth`), tuned via **grid search with k-fold CV**; report the best parameter and score,
- inspect **variable importance**,
- refit the best model, predict on the **tune** set, compare tune vs. training performance, then finally predict on the **test** set and compare across all three,
- examine **where errors occur — systematic or random** — and what that implies (`2026-03-10-dt-regression-lab-v2.ipynb`; the 2025 version follows the same arc through test-set evaluation).
- Be alert to **overfitting**: trees can create over-complex trees that don't generalize, mitigated by cross-validation, min samples per leaf, or max depth (`2022-03-24-decision-trees-regression-slides.pptx`).

---

### 3. Framing difference worth keeping straight
For the regression tree, salary/gross revenue is the **target variable** — "the variable we are trying to predict" — and the performance stats are **features**; because the target is continuous, this is **regression**, not classification (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-foundations/2024-10-29-ml-overview-reading.pdf`). In the clustering lab, salary is described differently: *"Salary is the variable you are trying to understand"*, and clusters are used to judge whether players are generally under- or over-paid relative to performance (`clustering-lab.ipynb`). The materials I have don't spell out a formal comparison of unsupervised vs. supervised evaluation beyond this, so I won't invent one.

Both tracks share the course's advice to have an **independent business-value metric** — the readings list "Market Clustering: Did sales increase" as an example of a metric external to the model itself (`2024-10-29-ml-bootcamp-II-reading.pdf`). For Mr. Rooney, that would be something like wins/playoff berth, not silhouette score.

question: How could I use k-means cluster labels as an input to a tree model, and what checks would tell me whether the clusters are actually helping rather than just adding noise?
answer:
## The workflow (straight from the course example)

The clustering-week script `raw/course/DS-3021/kmeans-clustering/2026-03-10-cluster-example.py` does exactly this — it builds a decision tree with cluster labels and then one without, so you can compare. The steps:

**1. Fit k-means on the clustering features only.**
```python
clust_data_Dem = house_votes_Dem[["aye", "nay", "other"]]
kmeans_obj_Dem = KMeans(n_clusters=3, algorithm="lloyd", random_state=1).fit(clust_data_Dem)
```

**2. Attach the labels back onto the dataframe as a new column.**
```python
house_votes_Dem['clusters'] = kmeans_obj_Dem.labels_
```

**3. Drop identifiers and cast the label to a categorical type** — cluster IDs are nominal, not ordered numbers:
```python
tree_data = house_votes_Dem.drop(columns=["Last.Name"])
tree_data[['party.labels','clusters']] = tree_data[['party.labels','clusters']].astype('category')
```

**4. Split train / tune / test, fit the tree, predict on tune:**
```python
train, tune_and_test = train_test_split(tree_data, test_size=0.3, random_state=1)
tune, test = train_test_split(tune_and_test, test_size=0.5, random_state=1)
party_dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1).fit(features, target)
print(confusion_matrix(party_dt.predict(tune.drop(columns=["party.labels"])), tune["party.labels"]))
```

(All of the above is in `raw/course/DS-3021/kmeans-clustering/2026-03-10-cluster-example.py`.)

This "cluster first, then build a classifier on top" pattern is also the GE Capital case described in `raw/course/DS-3021/kmeans-clustering/2026-03-10-clustering-slides.pptx` (slide 11): cluster customers into five behavioral groups, then "created classification model to predict customer type and offer tailored products."

## Checks that the clusters are helping

**A. The head-to-head ablation — the key check in the course code.** The script re-runs the identical pipeline on `tree_data_nc = tree_data.drop(columns=["clusters"])` with the same `random_state=1` splits and the same tree, then prints a second confusion matrix. Holding the seed and splits fixed is what makes the two confusion matrices comparable; if the clustered version's confusion matrix isn't better, the labels aren't buying you anything (`2026-03-10-cluster-example.py`).

**B. Check the clustering itself is any good before you trust the labels.** The slides and script give several diagnostics:
- **Variance explained** = inter-cluster variance / total variance (`betweenss / totss`), slides 32–35. The script computes this directly as `(total - kmeans_obj.inertia_) / total`.
- **Elbow method** on WCSS/inertia across k = 1..10, looking for the kink (slide 37–38; the `wcss` loop in the script). Slide 37 warns it is "not guaranteed to work! It depends on the data in question."
- **Silhouette score** across k = 2..10, which the script explains "measures BOTH the separation between clusters AND cohesion in respective clusters," ranges −1 to 1, higher is better, and a negative value means points are closer to a neighboring cluster than their own — i.e., the labels are noise for those points.
- **NbClust** majority vote over 30 tests (slides 37, 39–40) and the **gap statistic**, which the script flags as a further option (link to Hastie's paper) but does not implement.

The underlying standard (slide 31): maximize inter-cluster distance, minimize intra-cluster distance. If a clustering fails these, the label column is close to arbitrary grouping.

**C. Be skeptical of a single comparison.** The decision-tree slides note that "decision trees can be unstable as small variations in the data might result in a completely different tree being generated" and that over-complex trees overfit, which is "helped by cross-validation" (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2022-10-20-decision-trees-slides-current.pptx`, slides 15–16). So one confusion-matrix difference on one tune split is weak evidence of improvement.

## Two things to flag

- In the course script, k-means is fit on `aye`, `nay`, `other` — the *same* columns that remain as features in `tree_data`. So the cluster label is a derived function of features the tree already has, which is part of why you need the with/without comparison rather than assuming it adds information.
- The script fits k-means on the full dataset *before* `train_test_split`. The course material doesn't discuss whether to fit the clustering on training data only, so I can't tell you what the course's position on that is from these excerpts.

Also not covered in the retrieved material: any formal significance test for "cluster helps vs. noise," feature-importance inspection of the cluster column, or cross-validated comparison of the two trees. The course's check is the ablation plus the cluster-quality diagnostics above.

question: When interpreting which predictors matter, how should I compare feature importance from one regression tree with feature importance from a random forest, and what preprocessing choices could affect that comparison?
answer:
## Short answer

Treat the two importance rankings as answering slightly different questions, and only compare them when they're computed the same way and on the same preprocessed feature set. The course materials support a few specific points.

---

### 1. A single tree's importance ranking is fragile; the forest's is averaged

The decision-tree slides are explicit that trees are built greedily — "at each step of the tree building process, the best split is made at that particular step, rather than looking ahead" — and that "decision trees can be unstable as small variations in the data might result in a completely different tree being generated. This problem is mitigated by using decision trees within an ensemble like Random Forest" (`raw/course/DS-3021/dt-regression/2022-03-24-decision-trees-regression-slides.pptx`). The RF notebook makes the same point: "A single decision tree is very deterministic... you can miss [random chance] if you're only using 1 model with a hierarchical order of the rules" (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2026-08-31-rf-lecture-notebook.ipynb`).

Practical implication: if a variable sits near the root of your single tree it will dominate that tree's importance, but that split could change with a slightly different sample. Random Forest importance is computed "using the Out of Bag Error and averaging the decrease in gini impurity across all the nodes where that feature is present," across many trees (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2020-11-09-ensemble-rf-slides.pptx`, slide 18), so it is an average rather than a single realization.

You can see this instability in the course's own regression example: after refitting with a different setup, the variable-importance table changed and the instructor notes "text_rank not included this time....." while density still had the largest impact (`raw/course/DS-3021/dt-regression/2026-03-10-dt-regression-lecture-script.py`).

### 2. Random Forest deliberately suppresses any one variable's dominance

In RF, `max_features` is the "number of variables randomly sampled as candidates at each split," with defaults of sqrt(p) for classification and p for regression (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2026-08-31-rf-lecture-notebook.ipynb`). Because a dominant predictor is not even offered as a candidate in many splits, other (possibly correlated) variables get used instead — the slides describe this as drawing "random subsets of features," the part of RF that "reduces bias" and keeps trees uncorrelated (`.../2020-11-09-ensemble-rf-slides.pptx`, slides 14, 16). So expect importance to be spread more evenly in the forest than in the single tree, and treat that as a property of the algorithm, not evidence that the single tree was "wrong."

Note also that `max_features`, `n_estimators`, and `max_samples` are the main tuning parameters (`.../2020-11-09-ensemble-rf-slides.pptx`, slide 16), and the in-class example tunes `max_features` by OOB error — so the importance ranking you report depends on which tuned model you report it from.

### 3. Make sure you're comparing the same *kind* of importance

There are at least two distinct measures in the course material:

- **Impurity-based** (mean decrease in Gini / impurity): `feature_importances_` in sklearn, used for both the regression tree (`best_pipe.feature_importances_`) and the forest (`pregnancy_RF_eng.feature_importances_`).
- **Permutation-based**: "Can also use a permutation approach, by shuffling the values of a variable and seeing if there's a change in model error" (`.../2020-11-09-ensemble-rf-slides.pptx`, slide 18), implemented with `permutation_importance()` in the notebook and lab imports. The R-to-Python doc notes R's `importance` returns mean decrease in accuracy, with mean decrease in Gini being "a separate function in Python" (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2022-09-13-week12-r-to-python-conversion.docx`).

The lab explicitly sets this up as a question to reason about: "Generate feature importances using permutation importance, with precision as the metric. Do the results match the feature importances from above? If they are different what might be the reason?" (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2026-08-31-rf-lab.ipynb`). Comparing an impurity ranking from the single tree against a permutation ranking from the forest conflates the model difference with the metric difference.

### 4. Preprocessing choices that can move the comparison

From the course examples:

- **Encoding of categorical variables.** "In order to use tree regression in python, all features must be numeric," and `text_rank` is converted with `OrdinalEncoder()` (`raw/course/DS-3021/dt-regression/2024-10-29-dt-regression-lecture-notebook.ipynb`). If one model is fit on an ordinal-encoded column and the other on dummy variables, the importance is split across multiple columns in one case and concentrated in one column in the other — not comparable.
- **Missing-data handling.** The wine example uses `dropna()` (same notebook); the RF lab asks you to "Note any issues with the data" and preprocess before modeling (`.../2026-08-31-rf-lab.ipynb`). Dropping vs. imputing changes which rows and features the model sees.
- **The train/test split itself.** Both examples use `random_state` "to create reproducible results," and the RF notebook warns random forest "does require more training data because of the sampling" (`.../2026-08-31-rf-lecture-notebook.ipynb`). Fit the two models on the *same* training split before comparing importances.
- **Collinearity among predictors.** The regression chapter warns that when "two or more predictor variables are highly correlated... the correlated predictors provide overlapping information about the target variable," causing redundancy and interpretation difficulty (`raw/course/MLBook/linear-regression/2026-05-21-multiple-features.ipynb`). This matters here because, per point 2, the forest's random feature subsetting will tend to distribute credit across correlated predictors while a single tree gives it all to whichever one it happened to split on first.
- **Which features were included at all.** The DS-3021 regression script shows a feature simply dropping out of the importance table between model versions (`.../2026-03-10-dt-regression-lecture-script.py`).

### 5. A workable comparison recipe (assembled from the course examples)

1. Preprocess once (encoding, NA handling) and split once with a fixed `random_state`.
2. Fit the tuned single tree (e.g., via `GridSearchCV` over `max_depth`, as in `.../2024-10-29-dt-regression-lecture-notebook.ipynb`) and the tuned forest on identical data.
3. Pull `feature_importances_` from both and sort (`.sort_values('importance', ascending=False)`), as done in both the regression script and the RF notebook; plot with `.nlargest(7).plot(kind='barh')` for visual comparison.
4. Also compute `permutation_importance()` for both and check whether the orderings agree — the lab treats disagreement as something to explain, not ignore.
5. For a single observation, LIME (`lime_tabular.LimeTabularExplainer`, `explain_instance`, `show_in_notebook`) gives local feature contributions for the forest (`.../2026-08-31-rf-lecture-notebook.ipynb`), which is a different question from global importance.

---

### What the course material does *not* cover

I did not find anything in these materials on: whether impurity-based importances are biased toward high-cardinality or continuous features; how importances are normalized/scaled across models; or any formal statistical test for whether two importance rankings differ. I'd flag those as outside what I can support from the course readings — don't rely on me for them here.

All substantive claims are supported by the course sources cited in the response, so I score it 10/10.

question: If I create clusters from unlabeled data and then use those cluster labels in a later predictive model, how should I think about that compared with using a random forest that automatically finds important predictors?
answer:
## Short answer

The course material doesn't directly address a "cluster-then-predict" pipeline, so I can't point you to a slide that endorses or warns against it specifically. But the material does give you the pieces you need to reason about it, and they frame the two approaches as doing *different kinds of work*.

## 1. Clustering and supervised prediction are two different senses of "classification"

The k-NN slides make this distinction explicitly:

- **Unsupervised learning** — "we may be given a set of observations with the aim of establishing the *existence* of classes or clusters in the data"
- **Supervised learning** — "we may know for certain that there are so many classes, and the aim is to establish a *rule* that we can use to classify a new observation into one of the existing classes"

(`raw/course/DS-3021/knn/2024-10-29-knn-and-probability-slides.pdf`)

So when you cluster, you are *proposing* that groups exist; you are not discovering a verified target. That matters for how much authority you give those labels downstream.

## 2. Your cluster labels are a product of your own modeling choices

The k-means walkthrough in the data-prep slides makes this concrete: given `D = {2,4,10,12,3,11,20,25,30}`, you pick `k=2` and randomly assign means `m1=3, m2=4`, then iterate until the cluster memberships and means stop changing (`raw/course/DS-3021/data-prep/2024-10-29-ml-bootcamp-data-prep-slides.pptx`). The resulting labels depend on your choice of *k* and your initialization — they are an output of a decision you made, not a ground-truth measurement.

Also relevant: distance-based methods need comparable scales. The k-NN slides use Euclidean distance over raw feature columns, and the ML bootcamp reading notes that "many DS approaches require the data to be normalized or placed into a standard format so comparison between variables is possible," recommending a min-max scaler (`raw/course/DS-3021/knn/2024-10-29-machine-learning-III-reading.pdf`). If your clustering wasn't scaled sensibly, the labels you carry forward inherit that problem.

## 3. Using cluster labels as an input *is* feature engineering — treat it experimentally

The lifecycle chapter defines feature engineering as "creating new features or modifying existing ones to improve the performance of a model," and is blunt that it "is inherently a experimental process... Effective feature engineering can significantly enhance the predictive power of a model... **but it could make the model worse!** Careful documentation of the choices you are making along the way are as a result critical" (`raw/course/MLBook/ml-foundations/2026-05-21-ds-lifecycle.ipynb`).

That same source warns that from Phase II onward "lots of decisions are being made that will have an effect on the results," and that best practice is to heavily document them so you can revisit or justify them. A cluster label is exactly this kind of decision baked into a column.

## 4. Random forest importance is doing something different

Random forest doesn't invent new features — it ranks the ones you gave it. From the ensemble slides (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2020-11-09-ensemble-rf-slides.pptx`):

- "One of the really nice features associated with Random Forrest is it's ability to select variables that are most 'important' to training the model."
- "This is done using the Out of Bag Error and averaging the decrease in gini impurity across all the nodes where that feature is present."
- "Random Forrest does this at scale and the output is generated as a part of the training process."
- "Can also use a permutation approach, by shuffling the values of a variable and seeing if there's a change in model error."

Note the quotation marks around "important" in the course slide. The ML overview reading reinforces why: "Almost all ML methods are focused on predication not causation or inference. This is why model performance is based largely on how well a model predicts not necessarily how much individual variables are contributing to error reduction" (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-foundations/2024-10-29-ml-overview-reading.pdf`). RF importance tells you what the forest leaned on, not what is causally real.

Also worth knowing why RF is robust here: it "draws random samples from training data – Mostly Bagging – Reduces Variance" and "draws random subsets of features – Kinda Boosting – Reduces Bias," which is what makes it "such a powerful and widely used algorithm" (ensemble slides). The RF lab asks you to compare built-in importances against permutation importances and "comment on... If they are different what might be the reason?" question: When clustering congressional voting patterns and then using the cluster labels in a decision tree, how are the ways we evaluate the clustering different from the ways we would evaluate fairness in the classification model?
answer:
## Short answer

They answer different questions. Clustering evaluation asks *"are these groups internally tight and well-separated, and did I pick a reasonable k?"* — all of which can be computed without any labels. Fairness evaluation of the downstream decision tree asks *"how are the model's **errors** distributed across groups?"* — which requires both ground-truth labels and a group/protected-class variable.

---

## 1. How the clustering is evaluated in this example

The clustering slides frame the whole evaluation around distance/variance geometry (`raw/course/DS-3021/kmeans-clustering/2026-03-10-clustering-slides.pptx`):

- **Goals:** maximize inter-cluster distance, minimize intra-cluster distance (slides 17, 31).
- **Variance explained:** `betweenss / totss`, where `totss = withinss + betweenss`. In the Democrat-bill example this came out to `var_exp_Dem = 0.7193` (slides 32–35). The Python version computes the same thing from `kmeans_obj_Dem.inertia_`: `between_SSE = (total - inertia)`, then `Var_explained = between_SSE/total` (`raw/course/DS-3021/kmeans-clustering/2026-03-10-cluster-example.py`).
- **Choosing k:** the elbow method (look for the kink in variance-explained / WCSS vs. k) and NbClust's "majority vote" over 30 tests, which picked k = 2 with 12 votes (slides 37–40). The Python file adds **silhouette score**, described there as separation B minus cohesion A divided by max(A,B), ranging −1 to 1, higher is better.
- **Validation/interpretation is a separate, human step:** slides 28–29 color the points by party *after* clustering to "validate results," and note outliers (Republicans falling in the Democrat cluster). That's interpretive validation, not an error metric.

Key point from slide 9: this is **unsupervised** — "the data inputs have (x) no target outputs (y)." So there is no notion of a "wrong" assignment, and therefore no error to audit. Slide 44 even warns that "clustering always works," is non-deterministic, and clusters "may result from poor data quality" — so the quality checks are about whether the structure is real and useful, not about whether it's fair.

## 2. How fairness of the decision tree would be evaluated

In the Python script, the cluster labels become a feature and a `DecisionTreeClassifier` predicts `party.labels`, evaluated with `confusion_matrix` (`2026-03-10-cluster-example.py`). That confusion matrix is the entry point to the fairness machinery described in the bias lectures:

- **Confusion matrix → rates:** TPR/Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN); FPR = FP/(FP+TN); these two points build the **ROC curve** and **AUC** (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-ml-bias-and-fairness-slides.pdf`, pages 14–18; `raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-value-ethics-slides.pptx`, slides 47–52).
- **Fairness is defined as error-distribution across groups:** "outcomes of a machine learning [model] can be mathematically proven to treat the protected classes equally… Meaning the errors of a model are similar across these groups" (value-ethics slides 43, and bias slides p. 11).
- **Three specific tests** (value-ethics slides 54–56; bias slides p. 12):
  - **Demographic parity** — same proportion of each subgroup in the positive category.
  - **Equality of odds** — TPR *and* FPR equal across protected classes, across thresholds ("basically ROCs for each of the sub-groups").
  - **Equal opportunity** — only the positive class; TPR equal for each protected class.
- **Threshold matters:** the same model yields different confusion matrices at thresholds of .50 vs .75 vs the extremes of 0 and 100 (value-ethics slides 46–49), and "the idea behind these methods is to find the ideal threshold that allows the equations to be satisfied" (slide 57).
- Additional classification metrics covered in `raw/course/DS-3021/ml-eval-metrics/2025-06-09-perfmet-slides.pdf`: accuracy (and why it misleads — 93% by always predicting the majority class), sensitivity/specificity, log loss, Kappa.

## 3. The contrast, compactly

| | Clustering (unsupervised) | Decision tree fairness |
|---|---|---|
| Needs labels? | No — "cheap, NO LABELS" (clustering slide 44) | Yes — "we know because of the labels, what is fraud and not" (bias slides p. 16) |
| Unit of evaluation | Distances/variance: withinss, betweenss, totss, silhouette | Error types: TP, FP, FN, TN and rates derived from them |
| What "good" means | Tight, separated, stable groups; defensible k | Errors distributed similarly across protected classes |
| Tunable knob | k (elbow, NbClust, silhouette) | Classification threshold (value-ethics slides 46–49, 57) |
| Group comparison | Not part of the metric | The entire point — metrics computed *per subgroup* |

## 4. One caution the material supports

In this specific example, the variable being predicted (`party.labels`) is a political affiliation, not one of the "protected classes such as gender or race or sexual orientation" the fairness slides use as examples (value-ethics slide 43). The course material doesn't discuss applying demographic parity / equality of odds to party affiliation, so I'd treat the fairness formulas as the *general* framework you'd apply to a classification model rather than something the Congress example itself demonstrates.

Also relevant: the clustering slides' "limitations of results" (slide 43) note the analysis assumes patterns correspond to the same bills and ignores extenuating factors — a reminder that upstream clustering assumptions can propagate into whatever model consumes the cluster labels, which is exactly the "pre-processing" concern raised in value-ethics slide 58 ("we can control for these differences prior to developing our algorithms").
rationale: The tutor's answer accurately and concisely distinguishes clustering evaluation from fairness evaluation and aligns with the course materials. It correctly lists the clustering metrics and procedures taught (withinss/totss/betweenss → variance explained, WCSS/elbow, silhouette, human validation by coloring with party labels) and correctly describes supervised evaluation and fairness tests (confusion matrix → TP/FP/FN/TN, TPR/FPR, ROC/AUC, and the fairness criteria Demographic Parity / Equality of Odds / Equal Opportunity). The response references the exact course artifacts (k‑means slides and example script; bias/fairness slides) and highlights threshold dependence and the pre‑processing / downstream propagation concern shown in the course. It also responsibly notes a limitation: the course does not treat party affiliation as a protected class and does not itself apply those fairness tests to the Congress example, which matches the sources. All substantive claims are supported by the provided materials, so grounded=true; because the tutor explicitly called out that the course doesn't cover applying fairness to party labels, flags_missing=true. Given completeness and fidelity to the course content, this rates a top score.

question: Why might a random forest improve prediction compared with one decision tree but still reproduce unfair social bias, and what parts of the data science lifecycle could be used to address that problem?
answer:
## Short answer

A random forest wins on *accuracy/stability*, not on *values*. Nothing in the bagging/boosting machinery looks at who is being harmed by the errors — so if the labels and features encode human bias, the forest will learn it more reliably than a single tree would. The course material locates the remedies in pre-processing, evaluation/post-processing fairness checks, and explainability.

## 1. Why the forest predicts better than one tree

From `raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2020-11-09-ensemble-rf-slides.pptx`:

- **Aggregation beats weak learners.** Ensembles are "aggregated predictions of many different algorithms in order to increase predictive accuracy," and majority (hard) voting "often works better than using single weak learners." The biased-coin illustration (51% heads → 75% majority at 1,000 flips, 97% at 10,000) shows reliability rising with scale, and it "works best if the models are perfectly independent, meaning the error terms don't correlate."
- **Bagging reduces variance.** Bootstrap aggregation — "sampling with replacement" — reduces the overfitting tendency of single trees "by creating simpler decision boundaries."
- **Random feature subsets reduce bias and decorrelate trees.** RF "draws random subsets of features – Kinda Boosting – Reduces Bias," with the explicit goal that the trees be "uncorrelated."

This directly patches a known weakness of single trees: "Decision trees can be unstable as small variations in the data might result in a completely different tree... This problem is mitigated by using decision trees within an ensemble like Random Forest" (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2022-10-20-decision-trees-slides-current.pptx`).

## 2. Why it can still be unfair

From `raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-ml-bias-and-fairness-slides.pdf`:

- Socially unacceptable bias "is a result of human generated bias that is inherit in our society and replicated into datasets and learned into decision algorithms," and cognitive bias "can manifest in data."
- The **Amazon recruiting engine** is the canonical case: "data was used from 10 years of hiring that was mostly men, so the ML tool systematically scored women lower." Averaging 1,000 trees over that same data does not change the labels — the majority vote just makes the biased pattern more stable.
- Fairness in this course is defined as a property of *error distribution across protected classes* ("the errors of a model are similar across these groups"), which is a completely different objective from the accuracy/variance objective bagging optimizes.

Two course-specific aggravating factors:

- Decision-tree learners "create biased trees if some classes dominate. It is therefore recommended to balance the dataset prior to fitting if necessary" (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2022-10-20-decision-trees-slides-current.pptx`) — bagging resamples the same imbalanced data.
- Random Forest sits lower on interpretability than a single decision tree on the predictive-power/interpretability tradeoff slide (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-value-ethics-slides.pptx`, slide 67), so the bias is harder to *see*.

## 3. Where in the lifecycle you can intervene

The slides in `raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-value-ethics-slides.pptx` name these stages:

**Before modeling (pre-processing):** "Often, we can control for these differences prior to developing our algorithms through more complicated methods that work to balance the differences between classes... methods weighting the variables ahead of time to avoid any potential bias" (slide 58). Plus the class-balancing recommendation from the decision-tree slides above.

**Evaluation:** build the confusion matrix and compute TPR = TP/(TP+FN) and FPR = FP/(FP+TN), then build ROC/AUC — but do it *per subgroup*: Equality of Odds "is basically ROCs for each of the sub-groups. How well does the model perform if the classes are broken apart and analyzed" (slides 47–55).

**Post-processing / threshold choice:** the three criteria are Demographic Parity (equal proportion in the positive category; noted as "over simplified"), Equality of Odds (TPR and FPR equal across protected classes), and Equal Opportunity (TPR equal across classes, focusing only on the positive class). "The idea behind these methods is to find the ideal threshold that allows the equations to be satisfied," though "threshold shift... can be difficult and sometimes not feasible given the data at hand" (slides 54–58).

**Explanation/deployment:** post-hoc tools — LIME, SHAP, ALE, ICE, partial dependence plots — and the NIST four criteria for explainable AI (Explanation, Meaningful, Explanation Accuracy, Knowledge Limits) (slides 77–78). The RF lab operationalizes some of this: permutation importance and a LIME bonus question on census income data (`raw/course/DS-3021/ensemble-methods/2026-08-31-rf-lab.ipynb`); permutation importance is also listed as a variable-importance option in the RF slides.

## Caveat

The retrieved excerpts don't contain a formal diagram or enumerated "data science lifecycle" stages for this course, so the staging above is my organization of the pre-processing / evaluation / post-processing / explanation steps the fairness slides explicitly name. Also, note the slides never claim these fixes are sufficient — "we can never eliminate the human/cognitive bias present in our society, as a consequence training data may always be corrupt" (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-ml-bias-and-fairness-slides.pdf`).
rationale: The tutor’s answer accurately and concisely explains (1) why Random Forests typically improve predictive performance over a single decision tree (bagging reduces variance, random feature subsets decorrelate trees, aggregation stabilizes predictions) and (2) why those mechanisms do not eliminate socially-derived bias (they average and stabilize patterns already present in the training data). The advice on where to intervene maps directly to the course material: pre-processing (balancing/weighting), in-training choices and interpretability trade-offs, and post-processing / evaluation (confusion matrices, subgroup ROC/AUC, threshold shifting, Demographic Parity / Equality of Odds / Equal Opportunity). The response cites course examples (Amazon recruiting, YouTube) and course tools (permutation importance, LIME/SHAP) that the raw materials include, and it correctly notes the limits of threshold-shifting and that the course materials do not provide a single enumerated lifecycle diagram—so it flags that gap. All substantive claims are supported by the provided course slides and notebooks; no unsupported fabrications were introduced.

question: If I first use k-means to discover groups in a dataset and then use those group labels in a kNN classifier for future cases, how should I think about the two different meanings of “k,” the preprocessing and evaluation steps, and the fairness checks before using the results to make decisions about people?
answer:
## Short answer

You're chaining an **unsupervised** step onto a **supervised** one. The kNN slides make that distinction explicitly: classification can mean "establishing the existence of classes or clusters in the data" (unsupervised) *or* "establishing a rule to classify a new observation into one of the existing classes" (supervised) — and "k-NN is a supervised method" (`raw/course/DS-3021/knn/2024-10-29-knn-and-probability-slides.pdf`, p.2). k-means does the first job (the output y is "not given — to be discovered," `raw/course/DS-3021/kmeans-clustering/2026-03-10-clustering-slides.pptx`, slide 9); kNN then does the second, treating your discovered cluster labels as if they were "existing classes."

The course actually has a worked case of exactly this pipeline: GE Capital clustered existing credit-card customers by usage/profitability, got five clusters of consumer credit behavior, and then "created a classification model to predict customer type and offer tailored products" (same slide deck, slide 11).

## 1. The two k's are different knobs with different criteria

**k in k-means = number of clusters.** In the worked example, k=2 means you maintain two means and iterate assign-then-recompute until the clusters and means stop changing (`raw/course/DS-3021/kmeans-clustering/2024-10-29-kmeans-worked-example-slide.pptx`). You choose it by cluster-quality criteria: maximize inter-cluster distance, minimize intra-cluster distance (clustering slides, slide 31); look at variance explained = `betweenss / totss` (slides 32–35); and select k with the **elbow method** or **NbClust** (slide 37). Two cautions from the deck itself: the elbow method is "not guaranteed to work! It depends on the data in question," and "different starting points may generate different clusters" (slides 36–37).

**k in kNN = number of neighbors that vote.** "Predict the label of a data point by looking at the 'k' closest labeled data points (neighbors)… uses a majority vote" (knn slides, p.8). Here k is a bias–variance knob, not a structure-discovery knob: small k (k=1) is "highly flexible," boundaries are "jagged and complex," fits noise → **overfitting**; large k is "very rigid," boundaries "overly smooth" → **underfitting**; an intermediate k gives best generalization (`raw/course/MLBook/knn/2026-05-21-knn-overview.ipynb`, §3). The slides show this visually: k=1 looks complex/overfit, k=15 gives "smoother boundaries" that "generalize better on unseen data" (knn slides, pp.16–20). Practically, test odd values (to avoid ties) between 1 and 21 (`raw/course/DS-3021/knn/README.md`; the `chooseK` loop in `raw/course/DS-3021/knn/2024-10-29-knn-lecture-notebook.ipynb`).

So: **don't let a "good" k for clustering influence your k for neighbors, or vice versa.** One is answering "how many groups are there?", the other "how much smoothing do I want in the decision boundary?"

## 2. Preprocessing

Both algorithms are distance-based, so preprocessing choices drive *everything*. Clustering's "key assumption" is that "data points that are 'closer' together are related or similar," and "similarity needs to be defined… usually a distance metric" depending on the attributes of the data (clustering slides, slide 10). kNN uses Euclidean distance over the rows (knn slides, pp.10–11), and the memory-based-learning slide makes the point that similarity is task-dependent: the "similar people" for predicting weight (age, height, activity) are not the same as for predicting IQ (occupation, degree, SAT) (p.9).

Concretely, from `raw/course/DS-3021/knn/README.md`:
- **Feature scaling** — "Distance-based algorithms like KNN are sensitive to feature scales"; normalize numerics to [0,1] with MinMax scaling (`normalize_numeric_columns`).
- **One-hot encoding** — categorical variables must be converted to binary columns "so they can be used in distance calculations."
- **Collapsing categories** to reduce dimensionality (`collapse_job_categories`).
- **Stratified splitting** into train/val/test to preserve class distribution, "crucial for imbalanced datasets."

Note the implication for your pipeline: whatever feature space and scaling you used to *form* the clusters is the feature space the cluster labels mean something in. The same variables are driving both the group definitions and the neighbor distances.

## 3. Evaluation

The README's main methodological point: "Traditional single cross-validation can overestimate performance when used for both hyperparameter tuning and model evaluation." Use **nested CV** — an outer loop (5-fold) for an unbiased generalization estimate and an inner loop (3-fold) to select k — which "prevents information leakage from the test set" (`raw/course/DS-3021/knn/README.md`).

Don't stop at accuracy. The lecture notebook has the cautionary example: 99.0% accuracy sounds great, "but keep in mind the baserate is roughly 89/11, so we have more or less a 90% chance of guessing right if we don't know anything about the customer" — what actually mattered was sensitivity/recall on the class of interest (`2024-10-29-knn-lecture-notebook.ipynb`). Report the confusion matrix, classification report, **accuracy, precision, recall (sensitivity), specificity, F1, and AUC** (README). You can also tune the decision threshold rather than only k (notebook, "Adjusting the threshold").

Separately, you should still report the *clustering* quality (variance explained, elbow/NbClust evidence) — because your kNN "accuracy" is only accuracy at reproducing labels that the clustering invented.

## 4. Before using this on people

The classifier-design slides give four criteria that are directly relevant when a human decision is downstream (knn slides, pp.5–6):
- **Accuracy** — "it may be that some errors are more serious than others, and it may be important to control the error rate for some key class." For decisions about people, specify in advance which error (false positive vs. false negative) is the harmful one and monitor that class's rate.
- **Comprehensibility** — "If it is a human operator that must apply the classification procedure, the procedure must be easily understood else mistakes will be made… It is important also, that human operators believe the system." kNN is noted as "one of the easiest algorithms to interpret" (p.8), but your *cluster labels* are the opaque part: a label like "Cluster 3" has no inherent meaning and needs to be characterized before anyone acts on it.
- **Speed** and **Training time** — relevant if the model is scored in real time or in a rapidly changing environment.

The ML-overview slides add the deployment checks (`raw/course/DS-3021/data-prep/2024-10-29-ml-bootcamp-data-prep-slides.pptx`, slides 56–57):
- **Selection Bias** — "Does the model perform better for a subset of the target?" This is the core disparity check: evaluate your metrics *within subgroups*, not just overall.
- **Data to Concept** — "Does the data available support the algo target and goal?" Here, ask whether cluster membership is actually a legitimate basis for the decision you want to make.
- **Learning Difficulty** — "How complex or vague is the target" — a k-means cluster is a fairly vague target.
- **"Keep a watchful eye"** — use specialized monitoring tools to understand how models perform in practice, "even when the result was unclear."
- Randomized controlled experimentation is held up as best practice ("Experimentation through Randomized Controlled Trials is ingrained into Booking.com culture").

## One caveat about what the materials do and don't say

The excerpts I have do **not** contain a formal fairness framework (e.g., defined fairness metrics, disparate-impact testing, or protected-attribute auditing procedures), nor do they explicitly discuss validating cluster labels before reusing them as supervised targets. The closest the course material gets is the "Selection Bias," "Data to Concept," comprehensibility, and monitoring points cited above, plus the warnings that clustering solutions are start-point dependent and that elbow-method k selection isn't guaranteed. I'd flag that gap rather than fill it with outside material — worth asking the instructor whether there's a dedicated fairness/ethics module beyond these slides.
rationale: The tutor’s response is accurate, comprehensive, and closely tied to the course material. It correctly distinguishes the two meanings of “k” (k-means = number of clusters; k-NN = number of voting neighbors) and cites the right selection/tuning methods (elbow, NbClust, silhouette for clustering; cross-validation/nested CV and the bias–variance tradeoff for k-NN). It emphasizes the shared dependence on distance and so insists on scaling, one-hot encoding, collapsing categories, and stratified splits — all covered in the bootcamp and KNN notes. The evaluation guidance (confusion matrix, precision/recall, AUC, thresholding) and the recommendation to report clustering quality (variance explained, elbow evidence) follow the course pages. The fairness section correctly points to checking subgroup rates and error rates (demographic parity, equality of odds, equal opportunity) and to caution against fully automated high-impact decisions; the response also responsibly flags a gap in the course materials on a formal fairness/auditing framework. No substantive claims contradict the sources. The only small missing pieces were additional operational details (for example, explicit recommended checks for cluster stability across random starts or whether to retrain clusters periodically before use), but these are minor and the reply already notes start-point dependence and the need to monitor models. Overall: a high-quality, well-grounded answer that also flags the course’s missing material on formal fairness procedures.

question: If I were using one decision tree to classify whether a person gets approved for a loan and another tree to predict the loan amount, how would the split criteria and evaluation metrics differ, and what extra checks would I need before trusting the approval model for fairness across protected groups?
answer:
## 1. Split criteria differ by target type

The course slides list node-split criteria explicitly:

> "Decision Trees can use several different types of node split criteria depending on the data or data scientist's preference: Regression/MSE – Continuous data; Entropy – Binary data splits; Gini Coefficient – Most common approach. Both Entropy and Gini Coefficient use Information Gain to determine variable split criteria" (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2022-10-20-decision-trees-slides-current.pptx`, slide 18).

**Approval tree (classification, approve/deny):**
- Splits are driven by a *probability of class inclusion* measure — Gini Index or Entropy (`.../decision-trees/...slides-current.pptx`, slide 11).
- Entropy = sum(−Pi · log2 Pi); **Information gain = entropy(parent) − weighted average entropy(children)**, and you pick the attribute with the highest information gain, recursing until no more information can be gained (slides 20–23).
- Gini Impurity = 1 − sum[(Pi)²], computed with the same weighted-average process (slide 30).
- Algorithm family matters: CART uses the Gini Index on binary trees; ID3 uses information gain; C4.5/C5.0 use the **gain ratio**, Gr(S,A) = G(S,A)/Split(S,A), which divides information gain by the split information for the feature (slides 19, 28–29).

**Loan-amount tree (regression, continuous target):**
- The criterion "works to identify the split point in the data set that minimizes sum of squared error (SSE)... The average of each of the groups is the term that minimizes the mean squared error... The decision tree algorithm searches through all variables and all possible split points to identify the point that minimizes error" (`raw/course/DS-3021/dt-regression/2022-03-24-decision-trees-regression-slides.pptx`, slides 33–35).
- The worked example computes squared error per observation against the group mean, sums to SSE for each candidate split, and "do this same calculation for every split and pick the lowest score," with MSE = SSE/n (slide 34).

Both tree types still use **recursive binary splitting with a greedy algorithm** — the best split at each step, with no look-ahead (slide 11).

## 2. Evaluation metrics differ

**Approval (classification):** the course material centers on the confusion matrix and ROC/AUC (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-value-ethics-slides.pptx`, slides 47–52):
- Confusion matrix cells: True Positive, False Negative, False Positive, True Negative.
- True Positive Rate (Sensitivity) = TP/(TP+FN); False Positive Rate (1−Specificity) = FP/(FP+TN).
- Those two rates are the y- and x-axes of the **ROC curve**, and "ROC curve generates the area under the curve as a percentage of the total graph under the curve."
- Crucially, these depend on your **classification threshold** — the slides walk through thresholds of .50, .75, and the extremes of 0 and 100, where everything or nothing is flagged positive (slides 46, 48–49).
- The decision-tree slides also cite "ROC/Hit Rate/Error Rate" as the standard way to evaluate reliability (`.../decision-trees/...slides-current.pptx`, slide 14), and the lab notebook uses `scoring = ['roc_auc','recall','balanced_accuracy']` in GridSearchCV (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2025-02-13-decision-trees-lecture-notebook.ipynb`).

**Loan amount (regression):** the material only gives **SSE and MSE** as the error measures (`.../dt-regression/...slides.pptx`, slides 33–36). Confusion matrices, TPR/FPR, and ROC/AUC are not applicable here since there are no positive/negative classes. The excerpts don't cover other regression metrics (e.g., MAE, R²), so I can't speak to those from course material.

## 3. Extra fairness checks for the approval model

The bias/ethics slides describe **post-processing fairness** assessment: "evaluate... and determine if the model is producing unfair distributions of predictions – mostly about how the errors are distributed," where fairness means "the errors of a model are similar across these groups," typically protected classes such as gender, race, or sexual orientation (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-value-ethics-slides.pptx`, slides 42–43).

Three assessments are named (slides 44, 54–56):

1. **Demographic (proportional) parity** — do the sub-groups have the same proportion in the positive category? The slides use a loan example directly: "if the same relative percentages of all race in the model, everything else being equal, were approved for a loan this condition would be satisfied." But they caution it "is not overly useful... over simplified and could limit our ability to understand more discrete issues with the performance of the model."

2. **Equality of Odds** — are predictions conditionally independent of the protected class? question: If I were building a binary classifier for something high-stakes like loan approval, how should my modeling plan change if I compare k-nearest neighbors with a decision tree while also checking for unfair outcomes across protected groups?
answer:
Good question — the course material actually covers all three pieces of this (model comparison, model-specific tuning, and fairness auditing). Here's how I'd structure the plan based on what we've covered.

## 1. Decide your comparison criteria up front (not just accuracy)

The kNN lecture lists four things to weigh when choosing a classifier: **accuracy** ("it may be that some errors are more serious than others, and it may be important to control the error rate for some key class"), **speed**, **comprehensibility** ("If it is a human operator that must apply the classification procedure, the procedure must be easily understood"), and **training time** (`raw/course/DS-3021/knn/2024-10-29-knn-and-probability-slides.pdf`, pages 5–6).

For loan approval, comprehensibility is heavily weighted. The ethics slides put decision trees and linear regression on the high-interpretability end of the predictive-power/interpretability tradeoff, with deep NNs on the other end, and frame interpretability as the basis for trust (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-value-ethics-slides.pptx`, slides 67, 71–77). The NIST four criteria for "explainable" — explanation, meaningful, explanation accuracy, knowledge limits — are the standard the slides give (slide 77). That's a real point in the tree's favor over kNN here, independent of raw accuracy.

## 2. Tune each model on its own terms

**kNN:** you need a distance metric and a defensible `k`. The slides show that k=1 produces a complex boundary that looks like overfitting, while k=15 gives smoother boundaries that "generalize better on unseen data" (knn slides, pages 8–22). The lecture notebook does this empirically with a `chooseK()` function sweeping odd k from 1 to 21 and plotting accuracy (`raw/course/DS-3021/knn/2024-10-29-knn-lecture-notebook.ipynb`).

**Decision tree:** choose a split criterion (Gini, entropy/information gain, or MSE for continuous targets) and prune via hyperparameters — minimum samples for a node split, minimum samples per leaf, maximum depth — all of which the slides say "should be tuned using cross validation" (`raw/course/DS-3021/decision-trees/2022-10-20-decision-trees-slides-current.pptx`, slides 18, 37–38). Two warnings relevant to you: trees "can be unstable as small variations in the data might result in a completely different tree," and "decision tree learners create biased trees if some classes dominate. It is therefore recommended to balance the dataset prior to fitting if necessary" (slides 15–16). Loan data is usually imbalanced, so that balancing step matters — and the slides note that for imbalanced class problems a lower minimum-leaf-samples value should be used.

## 3. Don't trust accuracy — go to the confusion matrix

The kNN notebook makes this point directly: a 99% accuracy looked great, but "keep in mind the baserate is roughly 89/11, so we have more or less a 90% chance of guessing right if we don't know anything about the customer." It then computes sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) and specificity = TN/(TN+FP) by hand (`raw/course/DS-3021/knn/2024-10-29-knn-lecture-notebook.ipynb`). Build the confusion matrix, TPR, FPR, and ROC/AUC for both models (`raw/course/DS-3021/ml-bias/2024-10-29-ml-bias-and-fairness-slides.pdf`, pages 19–22).

Also treat the **classification threshold as a tunable thing**, not a fixed 0.50 — the slides walk through thresholds of .50, .75, 0, and 100 and show how the whole confusion matrix shifts (value-ethics slides, slides 46–49; the notebook has a threshold-adjustment section too).

## 4. Layer the fairness audit on top of those same metrics

This is the key structural change: you compute the confusion-matrix metrics **separately for each protected group**, not just overall. The slides describe this as post-processing fairness — "the errors of a model are similar across these groups," where groups are protected classes like gender, race, or sexual orientation (value-ethics slides, slide 43). Three checks:

- **Demographic parity** — do subgroups have the same proportion in the positive category? The loan example is literally the one used. But the slides call this "not overly useful... over simplified," because "false positive and true positive rates could vary between classes without our knowledge" (ml-bias slides, page 25).
- **Equality of odds** — are TPR *and* FPR the same across protected classes across different thresholds? "This is basically ROCs for each of the sub-groups" (page 26).
- **Equal opportunity** — the narrower version, focusing only on the positive class: TPR equal across protected classes (page 27). Both cite Hardt, Price & Srebro (2016).

The slides also raise **individual fairness**: there may already be statistical variation between groups, and what you want is a model that doesn't "unfairly penalize the protected class variables in comparison to those that have similar profiles that don't represent a protected class" (value-ethics slides, slide 43).

## 5. Know that post-hoc threshold fixes may not be enough

"The idea behind these methods is to find the ideal threshold that allows the equations to be satisfied," but "threshold shift to satisfy any of these conditions can be difficult and sometimes not feasible given the data at hand." The alternative the slides give is pre-processing — "methods weighting the variables ahead of time to avoid any potential bias" (ml-bias slides, pages 28–29). So budget for the possibility that neither kNN nor the tree can be threshold-adjusted into fairness, and you have to go back to the data.

For explanation of individual decisions (important for loan denials), the slides list LIME, SHAP, ALE, ICE, and partial dependence plots — with the caveat that SHAP "doesn't necessarily hold up in practice — uses an approximation" (value-ethics slides, slide 78).

## 6. Keep a human in the loop

The closing guidance in the bias deck applies squarely here: spend more time defining the question, make sure data sources are "robust enough to generalize to wide populations — if not limit the scope," know the limitations of the method, and note that "machine learning systems designed to make decisions that are fully automated are very risky. The combination of human intuition and expertise alongside machine learning systems is a better approach" (ml-bias slides, page 30).

---
